title: A Language for the Postcards
premise: After her mother's funeral, Jude Crane returns to the coastal house to catalog a lifetime of unspoken things—postcards never sent, letters never opened—when a letter arrives from Edele Voss, the last fluent speaker of Kessari, a dying language her mother secretly studied. As Jude becomes Edele's final student, the language's grammar of indirection mirrors their own family's silence, and they begin to understand what their mother was trying to say for thirty years. The climax comes when Jude must ask the forbidden question—about the sibling given away, the one the whole family arranged itself around—before Edele's memory fails and the language dies with it. In the end, Jude records Edele's last stories, writes the postcard their mother never sent, and mails it to the brother in Lisbon, choosing speech over inheritance of silence.
about_author: Juniper Okonkwo is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging endangered-language recordings before turning to fiction. She writes from a house full of unsent postcards, and this is her second novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Silence
chapters.summary: Jude, third-person limited, sorts through their mother Miriam's belongings after the funeral, finding drawers of blank postcards and a locked cedar box. The emotional beat is numb grief sharpening into unease: the house feels arranged around an absence Jude can't name.

chapters.title: A Letter in a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: Among Miriam's papers Jude finds correspondence in an unknown script, addressed to someone named Edele Voss. POV Jude. The beat is curiosity overtaking avoidance—the first crack in fifteen years of practiced not-asking.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Jude tracks Edele Voss to a fading seaside town and finds a woman in her nineties who says she's been waiting: 'Your mother promised me a student.' POV Jude. The beat is being claimed by something larger than grief.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Edele begins teaching Kessari, a language whose grammar has no direct word for 'I'—only 'the one speaking.' POV Jude. The beat is disorientation turning into strange relief; a language built for people who couldn't say things plainly.

chapters.title: What the Aunts Knew
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Miriam's voice via journal fragments: young Miriam hiding her linguistic studies from a disapproving household. The beat is the discovery that silence was inherited, taught, perfected across generations.

chapters.title: The Cedar Box
chapters.summary: Jude finally opens the locked box: photographs of a second child, a boy, dated thirty years ago. POV Jude. The beat is vertigo—the family's architecture of avoidance suddenly has a shape and a name half-legible on the back.

chapters.title: Grammar of Avoidance
chapters.summary: Lessons continue; Edele teaches the subjunctive forms used 'when the truth would break the table.' POV Jude. The beat is recognition—Jude maps Kessari's evasions onto their own family's choreography of not-saying.

chapters.title: The Brother in Lisbon
chapters.summary: Jue finds an address: Tomás Crane, Lisbon. They draft seven postcards and send none. POV Jude. The beat is fear masquerading as courtesy; the old art of almost saying it, practiced again.

chapters.title: Edele's War
chapters.summary: Edele recounts losing her own family to history and why she refused to teach anyone after 1974—until Miriam wrote to her. POV alternates Jude and Edele's told memories. The beat is two silences recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Miriam's Postcards
chapters.summary: Jude discovers the blank postcards were once written—drafts hidden inside book spines, all addressed to Tomás, none sent. POV Jude. The beat is heartbreak: their mother was also a student of almost.

chapters.title: The Question Takes Shape
chapters.summary: Edele's memory begins slipping; she confuses decades, calls Jude by Miriam's name. POV Jude. The beat is urgency compressing into dread—there is a deadline now, biological and linguistic at once.

chapters.title: Interruptions
chapters.summary: Jude's partner Dana arrives, pushing them to either commit to the recording project or come home. POV Jude. The beat is friction between the life Jude built to stay invisible and the self emerging through Kessari.

chapters.title: The Word for Grief That Waits
chapters.summary: Edele teaches a Kessari term with no English equivalent: mourning postponed until the question is asked. POV Jude. The beat is devastating clarity—Jude realizes their entire life has been lived in that tense.

chapters.title: What Miriam Promised
chapters.summary: Reading further letters, Jude learns Miriam promised Edele a student in exchange for help finding Tomás—and then broke the promise out of fear. POV Jude. The beat is anger at the mother, complicated by pity.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: A storm floods the coastal road; Edele refuses evacuation, insisting the lessons finish first. POV Jude. The beat is external stakes mirroring internal ones—time literally rising around the last speaker.

chapters.title: The Recording Sessions
chapters.summary: Jude begins systematically recording Edele's stories, songs, grammar—building the archive Miriam never made. POV Jude. The beat is purpose replacing paralysis; devotion as a form of asking.

chapters.title: Tomás Answers
chapters.summary: On impulse, Jude finally mails one postcard—their mother's draft, unsigned. Days later, a call comes: Tomás knew about Jude all along. POV Jude. The beat is shock dissolving into grief for thirty lost years.

chapters.title: The Question Asked
chapters.summary: Climax: with Edele lucid one last evening, Jude asks in Kessari the question the family arranged itself around—why was Tomás given away? Edele answers with Miriam's own recorded confession, made decades ago. POV Jude. The beat is the truth breaking the table, and the table holding anyway.

chapters.title: After the Table Breaks
chapters.summary: Jude sits with the confession: Miriam gave up Tomás under family pressure and spent her life unable to name it. POV Jude. The beat is sorrow without absolution yet—grief finally in the right tense.

chapters.title: The Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Edele, memory nearly gone, teaches one final phrase and mistakes Jude for Miriam—then, briefly, knows exactly who they are and says goodbye. POV Jude. The beat is tenderness at the edge of loss; the language passing hands.

chapters.title: What the Archive Holds
chapters.summary: Jude completes the recordings, deposits them with a language institute, and finds peace in the work's incompleteness—a language lives only while spoken. POV Jude. The beat is acceptance: inheritance redefined as obligation to speak.

chapters.title: Postcard, Sent
chapters.summary: In Lisbon, Jude meets Tomás at a café, speaks the first Kessari sentence Edele taught them—'I am the one speaking'—and gives him his mother's words. POV Jude. The beat is quiet resolution: the silence ends not with an answer but with a voice, finally, in use.
